lead: A design is judged by numbers: what one unit costs, how fast it answers, how much power it draws. These numbers are design metrics, or figures of merit. Every project has several at once, and a change that improves one usually worsens another. Engineers use the metrics to compare two architectures before building either one. The same list explains the hard choices of embedded design: fitting a deadline, a battery and a price into one small board.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 and Chapter 1.2: the device class tells you which metrics dominate.

blocks.text: Unit cost is the money to make one finished device. It has two parts. NRE (non-recurring engineering) is the one-time cost of design, tooling and masks, in rupees. Recurring cost is the parts plus assembly for each unit, also in rupees. If q units are built, the unit cost is NRE/q + recurring cost. The division is the point: NRE is paid once and spread over the whole run.
unit cost = NRE / q + recurring cost
blocks.where: NRE is the one-time design cost in rupees; q is the number of units built; recurring cost is the parts and assembly cost per unit in rupees.

blocks.text: At q = 200, an SoC (system on chip) with NRE ₹5,00,000 and recurring ₹300 costs 500000/200 + 300 = ₹2,800. At q = 2,000 the same design costs ₹550. The recurring cost did not change; the NRE share fell. An FPGA (field-programmable gate array) design with NRE ₹1,00,000 and recurring ₹800 costs ₹1,300 at 200 units and ₹850 at 2,000. The two lines cross at 800 units: below that the FPGA wins, above it the SoC wins.

sections.h3: Speed, energy and the other metrics

blocks.text: Performance is not one number. Throughput is work done per second, in operations per second. Latency is the time from an input to the matching output, in milliseconds (ms) or microseconds (µs). Deadline margin is the spare time before a required deadline; a margin of zero passes only if nothing goes wrong.

blocks.where: P is dynamic power in watts; C is the switched capacitance in farads; V is the supply voltage in volts; f is the clock frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: Static power is leakage, drawn even when the clock is stopped. Energy is power multiplied by time; battery life = energy available / average power. Size and weight matter in a wearable or a drone. Flexibility is how easily the function changes in the field. Reliability is the chance of working for a stated time. Safety is doing no harm when it fails. Security is resisting an attacker. Maintainability is the cost of diagnosis and repair. Correctness is doing the specified job for every allowed input. Each metric has a unit; a claim without a unit is not a specification.

sections.h3: Design challenges and the trade-off rule

blocks.text: The first design challenge is the hardware-software split: which functions go in fixed hardware, which in software on a processor. Fixed hardware is fast and low power but cannot change; software is flexible but slower. The second is meeting deadlines with the cheapest legal part: a part that is fast enough but has little flash or RAM is not legal. Code must fit in flash memory and data in RAM, with room for later fixes. A battery device needs a power budget: sum the current of every block, multiply by voltage to get total watts, then multiply the average watts by the required run time to get energy in watt-hours and compare that with the battery's energy rating. Choosing a processor before good compilers exist is a real risk; check that a compiler, debugger and libraries are available before committing. Testing a board with no screen or keyboard needs a debug port, a test fixture or boundary scan. Field firmware upgrade needs a bootloader and a safe recovery path if power fails during the update. Safety and security add verification cost.

Of cost, performance and power you can usually improve two at the expense of the third. A faster clock raises throughput and power. A cheaper part may miss a deadline. Rising IC design cost makes platform choice a business decision: a high-NRE chip is sensible only if the volume is large enough to spread it.
The architecture that delivers these numbers is the subject of Chapter 1.4 and Chapter 1.5.

figure.caption: Unit cost falls as quantity rises; the high-NRE curve crosses below the low-NRE curve at 800 units. Below 800 units the FPGA is cheaper per unit, above it the SoC is.

spec.aria: Two falling curves of unit cost against quantity; the high-NRE curve starts far above the low-NRE curve and crosses below it at 800 units.

examples.question: Design A uses an SoC: NRE ₹5,00,000, recurring cost ₹300 per unit. Design B uses an FPGA: NRE ₹1,00,000, recurring cost ₹800 per unit. (a) Find the unit cost of each at 200 units. (b) Find the unit cost of each at 2,000 units. (c) Find the quantity at which they are equal.
steps: Unit cost formula: unit cost = NRE/q + recurring cost.
examples.answer: At 200 units the FPGA costs ₹1,300 per unit against ₹2,800 for the SoC; at 2,000 units the SoC costs ₹550 against ₹850; the two are equal at 800 units, so build on the FPGA below 800 units and on the SoC above 800 units.

traps: Forgetting to divide NRE by quantity and treating it as a per-unit cost; NRE is paid once, so at quantity q its share is NRE/q.
Comparing unit costs at different quantities, or at quantity 1; the fair comparison is at the same q.
Mixing power and energy: P = C·V²·f is power in watts; battery life uses energy, so divide available energy by average power.
Using throughput as latency: throughput counts operations per second, latency is the delay of one operation from input to output.
Assuming a lower recurring cost always wins; at low volume a higher-NRE design can cost far more per unit.

quiz.q: Define NRE and give its unit.
quiz.a: NRE is non-recurring engineering, the one-time design and tooling cost, measured in rupees.

quiz.q: Unit cost falls as quantity rises even when recurring cost is fixed. Why?
quiz.a: Unit cost = NRE/q + recurring cost. NRE is fixed, so as q rises the term NRE/q falls and the fixed design cost is spread over more units.

quiz.q: A board has NRE ₹8,00,000 and recurring cost ₹250 per unit. Find the unit cost at 4,000 units.
A chip has switched capacitance C = 20 nF, supply V = 3.3 V and clock f = 10 MHz. Find its dynamic power.
Design A: NRE ₹10,00,000, recurring ₹200. Design B: NRE ₹2,00,000, recurring ₹600. Find the equal-cost quantity and say which design wins below and above it.
quiz.a: 1000000/q + 200 = 200000/q + 600, so 800000/q = 400 and q = 2000 units. Below 2000 units B has lower unit cost; above 2000 units A has lower unit cost.

quiz.q: A wearable has a small battery. Name two pairs of metrics that conflict and explain one pair.
quiz.a: Performance versus power: a faster clock raises dynamic power. Size versus battery life: a larger battery lasts longer but adds weight. Flexibility versus power: extra software features can fit in less fixed hardware but need more energy to run.

quiz.q: List three design challenges of an embedded project.
quiz.a: Any three: choosing the hardware-software split; meeting deadlines with the cheapest legal part; fitting code in flash and data in RAM; keeping within a power budget; testing without a screen or keyboard; field firmware upgrade; safety and security.

quiz.q: State the trade-off rule for cost, performance and power.
quiz.a: Of cost, performance and power you can usually improve two at the expense of the third.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses model-based cost estimation and power-profiling tools before a board is built. Platform selection often depends on software ecosystems and long-term part availability, not only on unit cost. Researchers study approximate computing, where a small correctness loss buys large energy savings. Search next for design space exploration, hardware-software partitioning, and energy harvesting.
